Stride and boogie-woogie are the two great left hands of early jazz piano. Both are solo piano music
for dancing, both swing, and both make the pianist's left hand do the work of a bass player and a
rhythm guitarist at once. They do it in opposite ways: stride **leaps**, boogie-woogie **walks**. This
page plays them on the band one at a time, then side by side, then swaps their parts.

How the examples work: press ▶ Play, switch players in and out with the buttons beside it, and read
what the band will play on the staff underneath: the whole pass is written out when Play starts, before it sounds. The tempo slider at the bottom of the page slows
everything down. For the history of each, see the Style Notes on [Stride piano](../styles/stride.qmd)
and [Boogie-woogie](../styles/boogie.qmd).

## 1. Where they meet

- **Rent parties.** In the 1920s, tenants in Harlem and on Chicago's South Side paid the rent by
  throwing a party with food, drink and a pianist. Harlem's pianists played stride; Chicago's played
  boogie-woogie. One piano had to be the whole band.
- **The left hand keeps time.** In both, the left hand never stops and never changes its pattern
  much. The right hand is free to play the tune, riffs and runs on top.
- **Swing eighths.** Both are swung: the eighth notes go long-short.
- **The same players.** Count Basie began as a stride pianist taught by Fats Waller, and his band
  recorded *Boogie Woogie* in 1936. Fats Waller played boogie-woogie too, and the boogie-woogie
  pianists knew stride.
- **Where they went.** Stride turned into swing piano (Teddy Wilson, Art Tatum, Basie); boogie-woogie
  into jump blues and rock and roll.

## 2. Stride: bass, chord, bass, chord

The stride left hand plays a low bass note on beats 1 and 3 and a chord in the middle of the
keyboard on 2 and 4. Here the band's pianist plays only that left hand. Compare it with plain
boom-chick, where the bass note is left to the bass player.

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="stride" data-chart="C|A7|D7|G7" data-tempo="100" data-on="comp" data-staves="comp" data-comp="piano" data-choice-label="Left hand:" data-choices='[{"label":"Stride","opts":{"compRhythm":"stride"}},{"label":"Boom-chick (chords only)","opts":{"compRhythm":"oompah"}}]'></div>

**What to look for.** On the staff the left hand jumps about two octaves on every beat. Stride
pianists practise the jump with their eyes on the landing note: the low one. Start with the root on 1
and 3, then play the fifth on 3. Full lesson: [Stride](patterns/chords-stride.qmd).

## 3. Boogie-woogie: eight to the bar

The boogie-woogie left hand walks up the chord and back down in swung eighth notes: root, 3rd, 5th,
6th, flat 7th, 6th, 5th, 3rd. The band gives it to the bass player. Compare it with the simpler lines
it is built from.

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="boogie" data-chart="C7|C7|F7|C7" data-tempo="100" data-on="bass" data-staves="bass" data-choice-label="Left hand:" data-choices='[{"label":"Boogie-woogie","opts":{"bassFeel":"boogie"}},{"label":"Chord tones, one a beat","opts":{"bassFeel":"arp"}},{"label":"Roots on every beat","opts":{"bassFeel":"roots"}}]'></div>

**What to look for.** The shape is the same on every chord; only the root moves. On the piano the
hand stays in one position, fingers 5 1 on the root and 6th. Full lesson:
[Boogie-woogie](patterns/bass-boogie.qmd).

## 4. Side by side on a blues

The same 12-bar blues in C, once in each style, with the whole band. Listen to the bottom of the band:
stride bounces between low and middle on the beats; boogie-woogie rolls along underneath in eighths.

**Stride**

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="stride" data-chart="C7|F7|C7|C7|F7|F7|C7|A7|D7|G7|C7 A7|D7 G7" data-tempo="132" data-on="bass comp drums" data-staves="comp bass"></div>

**Boogie-woogie**

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="boogie" data-chart="C7|F7|C7|C7|F7|F7|C7|C7|G7|F7|C7|G7" data-tempo="132" data-on="bass comp drums" data-staves="bass comp"></div>

The charts differ too. A stride player on a blues borrows the songs' turnarounds (A7, D7, G7 leading
home); a boogie-woogie player keeps to three chords, because the left hand is the interest.

## 5. Swap the parts

Both styles' parts can be played in the other's band. Below is the boogie-woogie band; swap its bass
and piano for stride's and back. The drums keep the shuffle.

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="boogie" data-chart="C7|C7|F7|C7" data-tempo="120" data-on="bass comp drums" data-staves="comp bass" data-choice-label="Bass and piano:" data-choices='[{"label":"Boogie-woogie","opts":{"bassFeel":"boogie","compRhythm":"boogie"}},{"label":"Stride","opts":{"bassFeel":"two","compRhythm":"stride"}},{"label":"Boogie bass under stride piano","opts":{"bassFeel":"boogie","compRhythm":"stride"}}]'></div>

The last one is busy: two left hands at once, one leaping, one walking. Real players choose one.

## 6. Before and after: ragtime and jump blues

Stride came from **ragtime**: the same left hand in straight eighths, under a written, syncopated
melody. Boogie-woogie went into **jump blues**: the same bass in a small band, with a hard backbeat on
the drums. Switch between each pair and listen for what changes and what stays.

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="ragtime" data-chart="C|C|G7|C" data-tempo="92" data-on="bass comp drums" data-staves="comp bass" data-choice-label="Style:" data-choices='[{"label":"Ragtime (straight)","opts":{"feel":"straight","groove":"boomchick","bassFeel":"alt"}},{"label":"Stride (swung)","opts":{"feel":"swing","groove":"auto","bassFeel":"two"}}]'></div>

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="jump" data-chart="C7|F7|C7|G7" data-tempo="160" data-on="bass comp drums" data-staves="drums bass" data-choice-label="Drums:" data-choices='[{"label":"Jump blues","opts":{"groove":"jump"}},{"label":"Boogie-woogie shuffle","opts":{"groove":"shuffle"}}]'></div>

See the Style Notes on [Ragtime](../styles/ragtime.qmd) and [Jump blues](../styles/jump.qmd).

## 7. Try it

- Pianists: switch the band's piano off in section 2 and play the stride left hand yourself, slowly.
  Then switch the bass off in section 3 and play the boogie line with your left hand.
- Bass players: the boogie-woogie line is a classic bass part in its own right. Play it on a 12-bar
  blues in section 4.
- Listen to Fats Waller's *Handful of Keys* and Albert Ammons's *Boogie Woogie Stomp* back to back.
